1 big thing: Don't call it a comeback
By Nathan Bomey
 

Jensen Huang, then serving as CEO of Nvidia, delivers the keynote address at the Nvidia GTC conference in Berlin in October. Photo: Alex Kraus/Bloomberg via Getty Images
 

A campaign to bring back Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia is gaining momentum — and has the support of President Trump — even as most analysts say it's out of the question.

The big picture: Certain employees, investors, and other corporate allies are calling on the Nvidia board to restore the AI titan as CEO despite his failings.

  • ✍️ Several thousand current Nvidia employees and others have signed a "Stand With Jensen" petition to bring him back.
  • 🏛️ When asked about the possibility this morning, Trump told reporters, "I would certainly not mind seeing that."
  • 🗣️ Elon Musk — a longtime Huang supporter — has publicly backed his return.

♟️ Zoom in: Huang himself "is considering a comeback" and has discussed the possibility with confidants, FT reported Sunday, citing multiple people familiar with the matter.

  • "One Huang ally told the FT they were putting together a 'war room' of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for the former Nvidia chief and would try to garner support from the White House," the FT said.

Reality check: CNBC reported today that the board is not considering bringing him back.

  • "There was a very good reason for him leaving — that reason hasn't changed," Charles Elson, a corporate governance expert and former University of Delaware professor, tells me.

📊 What they're saying: Kalshi traders were giving Huang a 14% chance of becoming Nvidia's next permanent CEO as this morning.

  • But those chances dropped back to 9% this afternoon after the CNBC report.

Even some of Huang's biggest fans have accepted his fate.

  • "The old Jensen with the black leather jacket and rock star persona is gone for good," tech bull and longtime analyst Dan Ives wrote in a research note. "That cannot be replicated and any talk of a damaged Jensen coming back to Nvidia is ridiculous in our view given the legal/Board/DC scrutiny/moral compass/China tentacles."

🍿 What's next: Nvidia will hold an investor conference call tomorrow afternoon to discuss its third-quarter results.

2. Closing the China chip loophole
 

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

Whoever is in charge of Nvidia in the long term may find it harder to sell chips to certain customers.

  • The Trump administration today moved to close a loophole that has given Chinese companies backdoor access to American AI computing power.

🇨🇳 How it works: U.S. export controls restrict the sale of certain advanced AI chips to China — but Chinese companies have accessed those chips by renting computing capacity from data centers in other countries.

  • The rule targets data centers abroad that supply "significant volumes of computing power" to companies in high risk countries, including China, Russia and Iran. The data centers have to vet their customers.

The big picture The action to close the loophole comes after mounting pressure on the Commerce Department to block a top U.S. adversary from accessing key technology in the AI race, Axios' Maria Curi writes.

  • Huang's affair with an Nvidia customer and alleged Chinese spy tied to Megaspeed — a data center company in Singapore — have intensified calls to tackle the diversion of chips to China.

🥊 The intrigue: The interim final rule was released by Commerce but "written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council," a press release states.

  • That language appears to nod to an ongoing and longstanding feud between Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and other top administration officials.

What we're watching: One of those officials is Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who took a shot at Huang yesterday, calling on Nvidia's board to select an outside CEO.

4. 🕔 After hours: Investment-grade Bond
 

Amazon MGM Studios released this image promoting Robert Pattinson as the new James Bond. Photo: Amazon
 

Bond — James Bond — will be Robert Pattinson.

State of play: Amazon MGM Studios announced today that Pattinson — the star, most recently, of the Chris Hansen crime thriller "Primetime" — will be the next 007.

  • The pick comes after an exhaustive search that also considered Callum Turner, Nicholas Hoult, Josh O'Connor and Jack Lowden, EW reported.
  • The 40-year-old Pattinson — who starred in "Twilight" years ago and, more recently, as Batman — is the "smart but safe choice," The Hollywood Reporter says.

What's next: "Dune" director Denis Villeneuve is directing the next Bond film, which is expected to arrive in 2028, per BBC.
